parts.note: layer reads as a stratum, but here it is a hen that lays eggs, a little breed famous for its fighting spirit

explanation.surface: A thin but durable coat of something, as of paint or rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer' suggests a stratum or coating; it is a laying hen, and the little hardy breed gave boxing its lightweight class name.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a small breed of domestic fowl, noted for pluck, and the hens lay eggs.

clue.text: Palm achieved in a race, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words a race are only one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Victory won in a contest, as palm means the prize of success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm' looks like the victor's prize, which fits 'achieved in a race'; it is the tree. 'perhaps' rearranges A RACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The areca is a tropical tree of the palm family, source of the betel nut.

parts.note: a cheat at cards is a swindler, and any card player who wins tricks could jokingly be called one too

explanation.surface: A guess that someone is a cheat at cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A deceiver or swindler, and a card sharp is such a cheat; the pun is on taking tricks at bridge or whist.

clue.text: She's a credit to the bowler

definitions.text: She's a credit to the bowler

parts.words: She's a credit to the bowler
parts.note: in cricket an over from which no runs are scored goes to the bowler's credit, and the young woman of the surface is the same word

explanation.surface: A woman praised as doing honour to a man in a bowler hat.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a MAIDEN over is one in which no runs are conceded, credited in the bowler's figures; 'bowler' also suggests the hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden is an unmarried girl, and in cricket a scoreless over credited to the bowler.

parts.note: a sure thing in racing slang is a dead cert, but read literally it is an event that certainly ends with someone killed

explanation.surface: Something guaranteed to happen, a racing tipster's sure thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatality is a death caused by accident or violence, so one that leaves somebody certainly dead.

clue.text: This should put an end to class distinction

definitions.text: This should put an end to class distinction

parts.words: This should put an end to class distinction
parts.note: the surface speaks of abolishing social rank, but the place meant is a school that gives refinement as the last stage of a girl's education

explanation.surface: A political promise to abolish the class system.
explanation.definitionFit: A private school polishing young women's manners was the final stage of schooling, imparting social distinction.

parts.note: Mavis looks like a woman being admired, but it is an old poetic name for the song thrush, which has another dialect name

explanation.surface: Someone admiring an attractive young woman called Mavis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is British slang for a young woman, so Mavis seems to be one; mavis is an old word for the song thrush.
explanation.definitionFit: Throstle and mavis are both old dialect or poetic names for the song thrush.

clue.text: But this shot could win at billiards

definitions.text: But this shot could win at billiards

parts.words: But this shot could win at billiards
parts.note: in billiards a losing hazard pots the cue ball off another ball and scores, so a shot named for failure can still win

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain stroke might take the billiards match.
explanation.walkthrough: In English billiards a losing hazard, where the cue ball goes into a pocket after hitting another ball, scores points.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is a losing hazard in billiards, a scoring stroke despite its name suggesting defeat.

clue.text: A domestic cross-patch, encountered on entering

definitions.text: A domestic cross-patch, encountered on entering

parts.words: A domestic cross-patch, encountered on entering
parts.note: a crosspatch is a grumpy person, but read as a patch of floor that is crossed at the doorway of a house it is the sill at the entrance

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered servant met as you come into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross-patch' means a grumpy person; split it, and it is the strip you cross when going into a home.
explanation.definitionFit: The doorsill or strip at the foot of a doorway, crossed when you come into a house.

clue.text: Little French one takes Reno return — he seeks divorce

parts.note: petit is French for little
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: return means the city name Reno is to be read backwards

parts.note: Reno, Nevada, was famous for quick divorces

explanation.surface: A small Frenchman heads to Reno, America's divorce capital, to end his marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns RENO into ONER; 'takes' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: One who files a petition with a court, here asking for the dissolution of a marriage.

clue.text: Victim of some lesser form of slavery

definitions.text: Victim of some lesser form of slavery

indicators.note: some means only a part of the words lesser form supplies the letters

explanation.surface: A person suffering under a milder type of bondage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks the letters from inside 'lesser form'; the whole clue also describes the answer, a feudal labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal labourer bound to the land, in a condition milder than outright slavery.

clue.text: Light armour ' churchmen need to combat it

definitions.text: Light armour ' churchmen need to combat it

parts.words: Light armour ' churchmen need to combat it
parts.note: the surface suggests light protective gear for clergy, but the Bible's armour of light is put on to fight its opposite

explanation.surface: Clergymen require lightweight armour for battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Romans 13:12 urges casting off the works of night and putting on the armour of light; the clergy fight the opposite of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence of light, and figuratively evil or ignorance, which the clergy strive against.

parts.note: a lock of hair is a tress

explanation.surface: Breaking open the second lock on a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like a verb about locks; it is the noun, and 'lock' is hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is pressure or strain exerted on a body, a physical force.

clue.text: This not in the furniture catalogue? That's the question

definitions.text: This not in the furniture catalogue? That's the question

parts.words: This not in the furniture catalogue? That's the question
parts.note: a ... is a stand of open shelves, so this word plus not is a furniture item, and alone it is the classic question word

explanation.surface: A shopper asking why an item is missing from the furniture catalogue.
explanation.walkthrough: A WHATNOT is a piece of furniture with open shelves; take the 'not' away and the remaining word is an interrogative.
explanation.definitionFit: An interrogative pronoun used to ask for information, the archetypal question word.

definitions.meaning: a haymaker is a wild swinging punch, which either lands or misses

explanation.surface: Weather chances for farmers getting the hay in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haymakers' suggests farm workers; it means wild swinging punches, which either connect or don't.
explanation.definitionFit: Haphazard and uncertain in outcome; a swinging punch may connect or fail to.

parts.note: conjurors' tricks are said to be done with smoke and mirrors, and a mirror shows a false image

explanation.surface: Asking what use a looking glass might be put to.
explanation.definitionFit: A deceptive appearance or false impression, such as a conjuring trick using reflections.

parts.note: a scrap is a fight, so a boxer's record of fights is jokingly an album of cuttings

explanation.surface: A boxer's daily journal.
explanation.definitionFit: An album for pasting cuttings and pictures; scrap is also slang for a fight, apt for a boxer.

parts.note: read as snobbish livestock it suggests posh cows, but it names the long-horned shaggy breed from northern Scotland

explanation.surface: Snooty farm animals that look down on others.
explanation.walkthrough: Highland cattle are a shaggy, long-horned breed from the Scottish Highlands; 'upper' hints at the high ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish breed of long-horned, shaggy cattle from the mountainous north.

definitions.meaning: mixing sugar or milk into a cup of tea with a spoon

explanation.surface: An afternoon tea that turns out thrilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Rousing and thrilling; also the act of mixing a cup of tea with a spoon.

clue.text: Sound way to travel on the Solent

indicators.note: sound says the next words are heard, not seen, so a word with the same pronunciation is wanted

parts.note: a ride is a way to travel, on horseback or in a vehicle

explanation.surface: A good way to cross the Solent by boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like 'reliable' and the Solent is itself a sound; it is the homophone signal. Ryde is a town on the Isle of Wight, facing the Solent strait off southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Ryde is a ferry port on the Isle of Wight's north coast, on the Solent.

clue.text: One of the Blues is able to hit back

parts.note: can means is able

indicators.note: back means the word for hit is read in reverse

parts.note: to bat is to hit

explanation.surface: A sportsman in blue who can strike back.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is a sportsman who has represented Oxford or Cambridge; a Cambridge man is a CANTAB. 'back' turns BAT into TAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cantab is a Cambridge graduate, and Cambridge sportsmen earn light blues.

clue.text: One thing to get out of a trunk

definitions.text: One thing to get out of a trunk

parts.words: One thing to get out of a trunk
parts.note: trunk suggests luggage to unpack, but a tree trunk sends out limbs

explanation.surface: Unpacking an item from a travelling chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb growing out from a tree's main stem.

definitions.meaning: a mark scratched to keep count, or a point scored

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick and his tally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name; it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A V-shaped cut, and a mark or point made in scoring.

definitions.meaning: Harry ... was a famous British music hall singer

explanation.surface: Praise for a top-notch variety-show artiste.
explanation.walkthrough: Music hall was British popular variety theatre; Harry Champion was one of its stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent, as in British slang; also the surname of music hall singer Harry Champion.

indicators.note: coated means the gold covers the article on both sides

parts.note: or is the heraldic term for gold
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A gilded item stands out from the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold-coated' reads as gilded, but 'coated' is the container signal: the heraldic gold wraps round the article.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinct or not the same as the one already mentioned.

parts.note: present-day suggests modern times, but it means a day on which presents are given, such as a birthday

explanation.surface: A complaint about modern entitlement.
explanation.definitionFit: A present, given on a birthday or at Christmas, which recipients anticipate.

clue.text: A sign, in writing, of ownership

definitions.text: A sign, in writing, of ownership

parts.words: A sign, in writing, of ownership
parts.note: a written mark showing possession, as in the cat's bowl

explanation.surface: A written document proving you own something.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark used before s to show possession.

indicators.note: to reform means the letters of lads hope are to be reshaped into something new

explanation.surface: A girl called Lily hopes her boys will mend their ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lily' looks like a name; it is the flower. 'to reform' rearranges LADS HOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: The asphodel is a plant of the lily family, linked in myth with the Elysian fields.

clue.text: Where they answer to the roll, call, no doubt

definitions.text: Where they answer to the roll, call, no doubt

parts.words: Where they answer to the roll, call, no doubt
parts.note: a roll call at school is suggested, but rolls here are bread, and the place supplies them

explanation.surface: A school register being taken as names are called.
explanation.definitionFit: A baker's shop, where bread rolls are made and sold, and customers call in.
